processing: An unoxidised green tea of young, even buds and leaves; the leaf is fixed and dried so it keeps its fresh colour. Details of the shaping vary by producer and are little documented.
harvest_season: Spring. As with other Chinese premium greens, the earliest and most tender pickings are the prized ones.
appearance_wet: Whole, fine shoots of even size, bright tender green.
taste_profile: Fresh, mellow and clean in the mouth, with a lasting clear aroma and a distinct note of chestnut.

brewing.notes: Typical handling for a tender green tea: a glass or porcelain cup, water well off the boil, and leaf left uncovered so it does not stew.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year spring tea, as is usual for Chinese greens, and best drunk within about a year. Early spring lots usually carry the premium.
description:
Fanjingshan Cuifeng is the protected-origin green tea of Yinjiang county in northeast Guizhou, on the western side of Fanjing Mountain, the highest peak of the Wuling range. The name means roughly 'green peak of Fanjing', and it also serves as the county's shared tea brand.

The leaf comes from gardens of the Fuding Dabai population, planted at 800 to 1300 metres. The climate here is mild and damp, with plenty of cloud and soft diffuse light, and the soils are acidic yellow and red earths. Tea people generally credit that kind of cool, overcast growing with a sweeter, more aromatic leaf.

In the cup, look for a clear lasting fragrance with chestnut showing through, and a fresh, mellow taste that finishes clean. Treat it like other tender spring greens: cooler water, a shorter steep than you think, and no lid on the cup.

Buying is mostly a matter of freshness and origin. Ask for this year's spring tea from Yinjiang, and expect the leaf to look even and clean rather than broken. Bright green, whole wet shoots after brewing are a good sign you bought what the label says.
history:
Local accounts say the green tea of Tuanlong village in Yongyi township, at the foot of the mountain and described as the tea's home, was sent to court as tribute under the Ming and Qing. Treat that as a regional tradition: no primary record is cited for it.

The modern product is better documented. Fanjingshan Cuifeng received national geographical indication protection from 9 December 2005 and took a run of prizes in Chinese tea contests from then on, including first prizes at the Zhongcha Cup. In 2009 a 200 g lot sold at public auction for 166,000 yuan, a price that says more about promotion than about the everyday tea.
